title: Antimicrobials: mechanisms, resistance & MDR drugs
subject: Pharmacology
anchor: Ribosome rule: 'buy AT 30, CCEL at 50' → Aminoglycosides, Tetracyclines on 30S; Chloramphenicol, Clindamycin, Erythromycin (macrolides), Linezolid on 50S
MRSA = mecA → PBP2a (low β-lactam affinity); VRE vanA = D-Ala-D-Lac (vanco + teicoplanin resistant)
Metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) = zinc enzyme, NOT inhibited by avibactam/relebactam/vaborbactam → ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam
algorithm:
Gram-negative isolate resistant to 3rd-gen cephalosporins
  ESBL (clavulanate-inhibited) → carbapenem (meropenem) for serious infection
  Carbapenem-resistant (CRE) → identify carbapenemase
    KPC (class A) → ceftazidime-avibactam / meropenem-vaborbactam / imipenem-relebactam
    OXA-48 (class D) → ceftazidime-avibactam
    NDM/VIM/IMP (class B, MBL) → ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam, or cefiderocol
  Salvage options → colistin/polymyxin B (nephro/neurotoxic), tigecycline (not for bacteraemia/UTI)

tables.title: Mechanism of action by class
head: Target
Drugs
Key point
rows: Bactericidal, time-dependent killing; aztreonam no cross-allergy with penicillins (except ceftazidime side chain)
Aminoglycosides: misreading, bactericidal, concentration-dependent, O₂-dependent uptake (no anaerobes)
Gyrase main target in Gram-negatives, topo IV in Gram-positives
Daptomycin inactivated by surfactant → not for pneumonia

tables.title: Resistance mechanisms & intrinsic resistance
head: Organism / enzyme
Mechanism
Consequence / answer
rows: All β-lactams fail except ceftaroline/ceftobiprole; vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin
High-level vanco + teicoplanin resistance (vanB: vanco only); linezolid/daptomycin
Class A / D / B (zinc MBL) carbapenemases
See algorithm; EDTA inhibits MBL (lab phenotypic test)

Klebsiella → ampicillin (chromosomal SHV-1); Enterococcus & Listeria → cephalosporins; Pseudomonas → ampicillin, ceftriaxone, ertapenem, tigecycline; Proteus/Providencia/Serratia → colistin; Stenotrophomonas → carbapenems

points: β-lactamase inhibitors: clavulanate, sulbactam, tazobactam (class A only); **avibactam** (A, C, some D incl. OXA-48), **relebactam** & **vaborbactam** (A, C; not OXA-48); none inhibit MBLs
**Aztreonam** is stable to MBLs but destroyed by co-produced ESBL/AmpC → pair it with avibactam
**Cefiderocol** = siderophore cephalosporin ('Trojan horse' via iron uptake), active vs MBL producers
**Colistin**: last-resort for CRE/Acinetobacter; nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity/NM blockade; plasmid **mcr-1** resistance
**Tigecycline**: glycylcycline, low serum and urine levels → avoid in bacteraemia and UTI; no Pseudomonas/Proteus cover; boxed warning ↑all-cause mortality
Concentration-dependent killing + post-antibiotic effect: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, daptomycin → once-daily aminoglycoside dosing
Imipenem is given with **cilastatin** (inhibits renal dehydropeptidase-I); imipenem lowers seizure threshold

ADRs: aminoglycosides oto/nephrotoxicity + NM block; fluoroquinolones tendon rupture, QT, avoid in children (cartilage); linezolid thrombocytopenia, serotonin syndrome (weak MAO inhibition), optic neuropathy; ceftriaxone biliary sludge, avoid with IV calcium in neonates; tetracyclines teeth/bone, photosensitivity, Fanconi (expired)

traps.stem: CRE isolate producing NDM-1; which single agent is reliably active?
traps.trap: Ceftazidime-avibactam — chosen because avibactam is 'the new carbapenemase inhibitor'
traps.fix: Avibactam does not inhibit metallo-β-lactamases. Use ceftazidime-avibactam PLUS aztreonam (or cefiderocol); MBLs are zinc enzymes inhibited only by chelators like EDTA

traps.stem: Pseudomonas susceptible to imipenem and meropenem; can ertapenem be used for step-down?
traps.fix: Ertapenem has no useful anti-Pseudomonas or Acinetobacter activity (intrinsic); also no Enterococcus cover

traps.stem: Enterococcus faecalis UTI reported 'ceftriaxone susceptible' by a junior lab
traps.fix: Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins (low-affinity PBPs); use ampicillin/amoxicillin or nitrofurantoin

cards.text: Ribosome mnemonic: 'buy AT 30' = {{c1::Aminoglycosides, Tetracyclines}} on 30S; 'CCEL at 50' = {{c2::Chloramphenicol, Clindamycin, Erythromycin, Linezolid}} on 50S

cards.front: Molecular basis of MRSA
cards.back: mecA gene (on SCCmec) encodes PBP2a with low affinity for β-lactams; ceftaroline/ceftobiprole still bind PBP2a

cards.front: vanA-type VRE: change in target?
cards.back: Terminal D-Ala-D-Ala replaced by D-Ala-D-Lac → vancomycin binding falls ~1000-fold; resistant to vancomycin and teicoplanin

cards.text: Avibactam, relebactam and vaborbactam do NOT inhibit {{c1::metallo-β-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP)}}; the combination for MBL producers is {{c2::ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam}}

cards.front: Why is tigecycline a poor choice for bacteraemia or UTI?
cards.back: Very large Vd → low serum and urinary concentrations; also inactive against Pseudomonas and Proteus

cards.front: Organism intrinsically resistant to ampicillin due to chromosomal SHV-1
cards.back: Klebsiella pneumoniae

verify: KD Tripathi 9e/Katzung 15e + IDSA AMR guidance 2024 (ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam for MBL)

title: Autonomic pharmacology: receptors, reversal & key drugs
subject: Pharmacology
anchor: Gq = α1, M1, M3 (IP₃/DAG, ↑Ca²⁺); Gi = α2, M2, D2 (↓cAMP); Gs = β1, β2, β3, D1 (↑cAMP); nicotinic = ligand-gated Na⁺/K⁺ channel
Adrenaline after an α-blocker → BP falls (unmasked β2 vasodilation) = Dale's vasomotor reversal; noradrenaline shows no reversal
Organophosphate: atropine titrated to dry chest; pralidoxime before 'ageing'; physostigmine reverses atropine poisoning

tables.title: Receptor → G-protein → key effect
head: Receptor
Second messenger
Key effects / drug
rows: Vasoconstriction, mydriasis (radial muscle), bladder neck contraction; prazosin, tamsulosin block
Bronchodilation, vasodilation, uterine relaxation, glycogenolysis, K⁺ into cells; salbutamol
M1 gastric/CNS; M3 glands, bronchoconstriction, detrusor, sphincter pupillae, endothelial NO
Nn ganglia + adrenal medulla; Nm motor end plate
D1 renal/mesenteric vasodilation; D2 pituitary (↓prolactin), CTZ

tables.title: Dopamine dose-response (adult)
head: Dose (μg/kg/min)
Receptor
Effect
rows: Renal/mesenteric vasodilation ('renal dose' – no proven renal protection)

points: **Dale's ACh experiment**: small dose ACh ↓BP (muscarinic); after atropine, large dose ACh ↑BP (nicotinic stimulation of ganglia + adrenal medulla)

Myasthenia: **edrophonium** (ultra-short) = Tensilon test, differentiates myasthenic (improves) from cholinergic crisis (worsens); **pyridostigmine** = maintenance; **neostigmine** (quaternary, no CNS entry) for reversal of NM block & crisis
**Physostigmine** is tertiary → crosses BBB → antidote for atropine/anticholinergic poisoning
Atropine poisoning: 'hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter'
**Pralidoxime** reactivates phosphorylated AChE only before ageing; not useful (classically contraindicated) in carbamate (carbaryl) poisoning
Atropinisation end-point = drying of bronchial secretions/clear chest (with HR > 80, SBP > 80), NOT pupil size

Glaucoma: prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost) ↑uveoscleral outflow, iris darkening/eyelash growth; timolol ↓aqueous (avoid in asthma/heart block); brimonidine α2 (avoid in infants – CNS depression); dorzolamide/acetazolamide CAI; pilocarpine ↑trabecular outflow (angle closure); netarsudil ROCK inhibitor
Atropine/mydriatics contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma; phenylephrine dilates without cycloplegia
Anaphylaxis: **adrenaline 0.5 mg IM** (1 mg/mL) anterolateral thigh in adults; glucagon if on β-blockers

traps.stem: An α-blocker is given and then adrenaline is injected; BP response?
traps.fix: BP falls — α blockade unmasks β2 vasodilation (Dale's vasomotor reversal). Noradrenaline (little β2) just shows a smaller rise; isoprenaline always lowers BP

traps.stem: Carbamate (carbaryl) insecticide poisoning; add pralidoxime?
traps.fix: Atropine alone; carbamylated enzyme regenerates spontaneously and oximes are not indicated (classically contraindicated for carbaryl)

traps.stem: Organophosphate patient on atropine: pupils still constricted but chest is clear and HR 110
traps.trap: Keep increasing atropine until pupils dilate
traps.fix: Endpoint is drying of secretions/clear chest; pupil size is not a target — risk of atropine toxicity

cards.text: α1, M1 and M3 couple to {{c1::Gq (IP₃/DAG)}}; α2 and M2 couple to {{c2::Gi (↓cAMP)}}

cards.front: Drug used to differentiate myasthenic from cholinergic crisis
cards.back: Edrophonium (short-acting anticholinesterase): myasthenic improves, cholinergic worsens

cards.front: Antidote for atropine (anticholinergic) poisoning and why this anticholinesterase
cards.back: Physostigmine – tertiary amine, crosses BBB, reverses central + peripheral effects

cards.text: Dopamine at > 10 μg/kg/min acts mainly on {{c1::α1}} receptors; at 2–10 μg/kg/min on {{c2::β1}}

cards.front: Antiglaucoma drug that causes iris hyperpigmentation and hypertrichosis of lashes
cards.back: Latanoprost (PGF2α analogue) – increases uveoscleral outflow

cards.front: Discriminator: Gq vs Gs vs Gi receptors?
cards.back: Gs (↑cAMP): β1, β2, D1, H2, V2. Gi (↓cAMP): α2, M2, D2. Gq (↑IP3/DAG/Ca²⁺): α1, M1, M3, H1, V1.

verify: KD Tripathi 9e; Dale's vasomotor reversal per Tripathi (adrenaline after α-blocker)

title: Anticoagulants, antiplatelets & thrombolytics
subject: Pharmacology
anchor: UFH: AT-III → IIa = Xa, aPTT, protamine; LMWH: Xa > IIa, anti-Xa level, partial protamine reversal
Warfarin: VKOR → ↓II, VII, IX, X, C, S; INR; vitamin K + 4-factor PCC
HIT: platelets fall > 50% day 5–10 + thrombosis → stop all heparin, start argatroban; no warfarin until platelets recover
algorithm:
Suspected HIT (4T score intermediate/high)
  → stop ALL heparin (incl. flushes, LMWH)
  → start non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban (hepatic clearance, use in renal failure) / bivalirudin / fondaparinux
  → send anti-PF4/heparin ELISA → confirm with functional assay (serotonin release)
  → avoid platelet transfusion routinely; if on warfarin give vitamin K (venous limb gangrene risk)
  → start warfarin only after platelets ≥ 150 × 10⁹/L, overlap ≥ 5 days

tables.title: Anticoagulant comparison
head: Drug
Target
Monitoring
Reversal
Notes
rows: IV/SC; HIT, osteoporosis, hyperkalaemia; safe in pregnancy & renal failure
Usually none; anti-Xa in renal failure, obesity, pregnancy
VKORC1 → ↓II, VII, IX, X, C, S
Vitamin K IV + 4F-PCC (FFP if PCC unavailable)
Fixed dose; not for mechanical valves or triple-positive APS

tables.title: Antiplatelets & thrombolytics
head: Drug
Mechanism
High-yield point
rows: Tenecteplase single bolus, most fibrin-specific; bleeding → tranexamic acid + cryoprecipitate

points: Heparin needs ≥ 18-saccharide chains to bridge AT-III and thrombin; short LMWH chains mainly inhibit Xa
**Warfarin skin necrosis**: early fall of protein C (short t½) → transient hypercoagulability; risk in protein C deficiency; overlap heparin ≥ 5 days and until INR ≥ 2 for 24 h
**Fetal warfarin syndrome** (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses) – weeks 6–12; heparin/LMWH preferred in pregnancy
Warfarin potentiated by enzyme inhibitors (metronidazole, fluconazole, amiodarone, cotrimoxazole); reduced by rifampicin, vitamin K-rich food
**Argatroban** is hepatically cleared (use in renal failure); bivalirudin mainly enzymatic/renal; both direct thrombin inhibitors
DOACs avoided in mechanical heart valves and triple-positive APS → warfarin
Cilostazol (PDE3) for intermittent claudication; contraindicated in heart failure
Thrombolysis window: STEMI ≤ 12 h; acute ischaemic stroke alteplase ≤ 4.5 h

traps.stem: Patient on fondaparinux bleeds; give protamine?
traps.fix: Protamine does not reverse fondaparinux (no long chain); supportive care ± rFVIIa. Protamine fully reverses UFH, only partially LMWH

traps.stem: HIT diagnosed; platelets 40 × 10⁹/L; start warfarin to 'get ahead'?
traps.fix: Warfarin during acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene (protein C drop); start only when platelets recover (≥ 150), with ≥ 5-day overlap

traps.stem: Major bleed on dabigatran – specific reversal?
traps.fix: Idarucizumab (Fab fragment) reverses dabigatran; andexanet alfa reverses Xa inhibitors

cards.text: Dabigatran is reversed by {{c1::idarucizumab}}; rivaroxaban/apixaban by {{c2::andexanet alfa}}

cards.front: Best lab test to monitor LMWH in pregnancy or renal failure
cards.back: Anti-factor Xa activity (aPTT is unreliable)

cards.front: Non-heparin anticoagulant of choice in HIT with renal failure
cards.back: Argatroban (direct thrombin inhibitor, hepatic clearance)

cards.text: Warfarin skin necrosis is due to early depletion of {{c1::protein C}}, which has a shorter half-life than factors {{c2::II, IX and X}}

cards.front: P2Y12 blocker that is reversible and not a prodrug
cards.back: Ticagrelor (also causes dyspnoea)

verify: ASH 2018 HIT guideline; CHEST antithrombotic guidance; KD Tripathi 9e

title: Anticancer drugs: toxicities, cell cycle, mAbs & TKIs
subject: Pharmacology
anchor: Toxicity → protector pairs: doxorubicin–dexrazoxane, cisplatin–amifostine, cyclophosphamide–mesna, methotrexate–leucovorin
Vincristine = neuropathy, marrow-sparing; vinblastine = marrow suppression; bleomycin = lung fibrosis, marrow-sparing
mAb suffix: -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanised, -umab human; checkpoint inhibitors → immune-related AEs treated with steroids

tables.title: Classic chemotherapy toxicities
head: Drug
Signature toxicity
Prevention / antidote
rows: Dilated cardiomyopathy (cumulative dose-dependent), red urine, radiation recall
Dexrazoxane (iron chelator); cap cumulative dose; echo/MUGA
Pulmonary fibrosis, skin pigmentation; little myelosuppression
Limit cumulative dose; avoid high FiO₂
Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue; glucarpidase in renal failure
Mucositis, diarrhoea, hand-foot syndrome; severe in DPD deficiency
LVEF monitoring; avoid with anthracycline concurrently

tables.title: Targeted therapy: mAbs & TKIs
head: Agent
Target
Use / unique AE
rows: B-cell NHL, CLL, RA; HBV reactivation, PML
Colorectal, NSCLC; hypertension, proteinuria, GI perforation, poor wound healing, bleeding
RAS wild-type colorectal, head & neck; acneiform rash, ↓Mg²⁺
Melanoma, NSCLC, MSI-high; colitis, thyroiditis, pneumonitis
Myeloma; panreactive antibody screen (interferes with cross-match)
CML, GIST; T315I mutation resistant → ponatinib/asciminib
NSCLC after gefitinib/erlotinib resistance (T790M), now first-line
CLL, mantle cell; atrial fibrillation, bleeding

points: Cell-cycle specific: **S** – antimetabolites (MTX, 5-FU, 6-MP, cytarabine, hydroxyurea), etoposide (S/G2, topo II); **G2** – bleomycin; **M** – vinca alkaloids, taxanes
Vinca alkaloids inhibit tubulin polymerisation; **taxanes** stabilise microtubules (prevent depolymerisation)
Cell-cycle non-specific: alkylating agents, platinum compounds, anthracyclines (largely), nitrosoureas
6-mercaptopurine/azathioprine dose must be cut to ~1/4–1/3 with **allopurinol** (xanthine oxidase); TPMT deficiency → severe myelotoxicity
Most emetogenic: cisplatin; prophylaxis = 5-HT₃ antagonist + NK1 antagonist (aprepitant) + dexamethasone
**CAR-T** (e.g., anti-CD19 tisagenlecleucel; India's indigenous NexCART-19 approved 2023): autologous T cells; cytokine release syndrome → **tocilizumab** (IL-6R); neurotoxicity (ICANS) → steroids
Imatinib resistance: T315I 'gatekeeper' mutation responds to ponatinib, not to dasatinib/nilotinib
Rituximab: screen HBsAg and anti-HBc before starting

traps.stem: Patient on 5-FU with severe mucositis: give leucovorin as rescue?
traps.fix: Leucovorin stabilises FdUMP–thymidylate synthase binding and ENHANCES 5-FU; it rescues methotrexate. 5-FU antidote = uridine triacetate

traps.stem: Child on vincristine develops foot drop and constipation; blood counts normal
traps.trap: Expect marrow suppression as dose-limiting toxicity
traps.fix: Vincristine is neurotoxic and marrow-sparing; vinblastine is the myelosuppressive vinca

traps.stem: Lung adenocarcinoma progresses on erlotinib; re-biopsy shows EGFR T790M
traps.fix: Osimertinib (third-generation EGFR TKI) is active against T790M

cards.text: Cyclophosphamide haemorrhagic cystitis is caused by {{c1::acrolein}} and prevented with {{c2::mesna}}

cards.front: Cardioprotectant used with doxorubicin
cards.back: Dexrazoxane (iron chelator, reduces free-radical injury)

cards.front: Target of ipilimumab vs pembrolizumab
cards.back: Ipilimumab = CTLA-4; pembrolizumab = PD-1 (nivolumab also PD-1; atezolizumab PD-L1)

cards.text: Blinatumomab is a bispecific T-cell engager binding {{c1::CD19}} on B cells and {{c2::CD3}} on T cells

cards.front: Drug of choice for CAR-T cytokine release syndrome
cards.back: Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor), plus steroids if severe

cards.front: Anticancer drug causing pulmonary fibrosis with minimal myelosuppression
cards.back: Bleomycin (lungs and skin lack bleomycin hydrolase)

verify: KD Tripathi 9e / Katzung 15e; NexCART-19 (actalycabtagene autoleucel) CDSCO approval Oct 2023

title: Pharmacokinetics, interactions, TDM & drug development
subject: Pharmacology
anchor: t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL; steady state in 4–5 half-lives regardless of dose
Loading dose depends on Vd; maintenance dose depends on clearance
Zero-order (saturation) kinetics: Phenytoin, Ethanol, Aspirin high dose ('PEA') → t½ rises with dose

tables.title: Core formulas
head: Parameter
Formula
Exam use
rows: High Vd (digoxin, chloroquine) → not removed by dialysis
CL = rate of elimination / plasma concentration
Time to steady state & to washout (4–5 t½)
Doubling dose doubles Css, not time to reach it
IV = 100%; bioequivalence: 90% CI of AUC/Cmax ratio within 80–125%

tables.title: Enzyme inducers vs inhibitors
head: Inducers (↓ effect of co-drugs)
Inhibitors (↑ toxicity of co-drugs)
rows: Acute alcohol, cimetidine, omeprazole (CYP2C19), isoniazid, valproate
Ritonavir, grapefruit juice (intestinal CYP3A4), amiodarone, metronidazole, disulfiram

points: Zero-order: constant AMOUNT eliminated per unit time; small dose increments → disproportionate rise in level (phenytoin)
First-order: constant FRACTION eliminated; t½ constant; most drugs

Classic interactions: rifampicin + OCP → contraceptive failure; clopidogrel + omeprazole → ↓activation; allopurinol + azathioprine/6-MP → marrow toxicity; ciprofloxacin + theophylline → seizures; sildenafil + nitrates → hypotension; MAOI + tyramine → hypertensive crisis; lithium + thiazide/NSAID/ACEi → lithium toxicity; probenecid + penicillin → beneficial ↑levels

**TDM** needed for narrow therapeutic index drugs with poor dose–response predictability: digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, cyclosporine/tacrolimus, theophylline, antiepileptics
TDM NOT useful: drugs with measurable effect (antihypertensives, hypoglycaemics, warfarin—INR), 'hit-and-run' drugs (omeprazole, MAOIs, reserpine), drugs acting via active metabolites

Trial phases: **0** microdosing (exploratory); **I** safety/PK/MTD in healthy volunteers (patients for anticancer drugs); **II** efficacy & dose-finding in small patient groups; **III** large multicentric RCTs for marketing approval; **IV** post-marketing surveillance
India: New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019 (replaced Schedule Y); approval by DCGI/CDSCO; ethics committee approval mandatory
**PvPI** launched 2010; National Coordination Centre = Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad; global database VigiBase at Uppsala Monitoring Centre (Sweden)
Causality: WHO-UMC scale, Naranjo algorithm; severity: Hartwig scale; Type A (augmented, dose-related) vs Type B (bizarre, idiosyncratic)

traps.stem: Dose of a first-order drug is doubled; how long to reach the new steady state?
traps.trap: Half the time, since the dose is larger
traps.fix: Still 4–5 half-lives; dose changes Css, not time to steady state. Only a loading dose shortens time to target

traps.stem: Phenytoin level subtherapeutic at 300 mg/day; increase to 600 mg/day?
traps.trap: Doubling dose doubles the level (linear kinetics)
traps.fix: Phenytoin shows saturation (zero-order) kinetics at therapeutic levels; small increments (e.g., 25–50 mg) cause disproportionate rises → toxicity

traps.stem: Which drug does not need TDM: lithium, digoxin, warfarin, gentamicin?
traps.fix: Warfarin is monitored by its effect (INR), not plasma levels; gentamicin needs trough/peak monitoring

cards.text: Loading dose depends on {{c1::volume of distribution}}; maintenance dose depends on {{c2::clearance}}

cards.front: Drugs following zero-order kinetics (classic trio)
cards.back: Phenytoin, ethanol, aspirin (high dose) – 'PEA'

cards.front: Post-marketing surveillance is which clinical trial phase?
cards.back: Phase IV

cards.text: Time to reach steady state ≈ {{c1::4–5}} half-lives and is {{c2::independent of the dose}}

cards.front: National Coordination Centre for PvPI
cards.back: Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad (PvPI launched 2010)

title: Systemic pharmacology: CNS, CVS & endocrine drugs of choice
subject: Pharmacology
anchor: Absence → ethosuximide/valproate (carbamazepine worsens); infantile spasms with tuberous sclerosis → vigabatrin
Pregnancy HTN → labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa; ACEi/ARB contraindicated
HFrEF four pillars: ARNI/ACEi/ARB + β-blocker + MRA + SGLT2 inhibitor

head: Situation
Drug of choice
Avoid / note
rows: Valproate (lamotrigine/levetiracetam in women of child-bearing age)
Valproate: neural tube defects, hepatotoxicity, weight gain, PCOS
ACTH / prednisolone; vigabatrin (DOC in tuberous sclerosis)
IV lorazepam (or diazepam/midazolam) → fosphenytoin / valproate / levetiracetam
Toxicity: loss of patellar reflex → calcium gluconate

tables.title: Vaughan-Williams antiarrhythmics
head: Class
Drugs
Key fact
rows: Quinidine cinchonism; procainamide drug-induced lupus; QT ↑
Amiodarone: pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid (hypo/hyper), corneal deposits, blue-grey skin, hepatotoxicity
Avoid verapamil in WPW with AF
Adenosine DOC for PSVT (t½ < 10 s); Mg²⁺ for torsades

points: Antiparkinson: levodopa + carbidopa (peripheral dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor); dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) → impulse-control disorders; MAO-B (selegiline, rasagiline); COMT (entacapone; tolcapone hepatotoxic); amantadine for dyskinesia; anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl) for **drug-induced parkinsonism**; use domperidone (not metoclopramide) for nausea

Antihypertensives: BPH → α1-blocker (prazosin/doxazosin); gout → losartan (uricosuric), avoid thiazides; diabetic nephropathy → ACEi/ARB; pheochromocytoma → phenoxybenzamine before β-blocker; aortic dissection → IV esmolol/labetalol; bilateral renal artery stenosis → ACEi contraindicated
Nitroprusside: cyanide toxicity → hydroxocobalamin / sodium thiosulfate

Heart failure: ivabradine (If blocker) if HR ≥ 70 in sinus rhythm; hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate if ACEi intolerant; digoxin & loop diuretics = symptomatic only; digoxin toxicity ↑ by hypokalaemia → digoxin Fab

Diabetes: metformin (lactic acidosis, B12 deficiency; avoid eGFR < 30); sulfonylureas (hypoglycaemia, weight gain); pioglitazone (fluid retention – avoid in HF, fractures); DPP-4 inhibitors (weight neutral); GLP-1 RA (weight loss; avoid with MTC/MEN2); SGLT2i (euglycaemic DKA, genital mycotic infection, Fournier gangrene; HF/CKD benefit); acarbose hypoglycaemia → treat with glucose, not sucrose
Insulin: only regular insulin is given IV (DKA); rapid = lispro, aspart, glulisine; long = glargine, detemir, degludec

Glucocorticoid potency: hydrocortisone 1, prednisolone 4, methylprednisolone 5, dexamethasone ~25 (negligible mineralocorticoid); fludrocortisone = mineralocorticoid; dexamethasone/betamethasone for fetal lung maturity

Thyroid: carbimazole/methimazole preferred except 1st trimester & thyroid storm (PTU – also blocks peripheral T4→T3; hepatotoxic); both cause agranulocytosis; iodine (Lugol) given ≥ 1 h after thionamide; radioiodine contraindicated in pregnancy

traps.stem: Child with absence seizures started on carbamazepine; spells increase
traps.fix: Carbamazepine/phenytoin aggravate absence and myoclonic seizures; switch to ethosuximide or valproate

traps.stem: Drug-induced parkinsonism from haloperidol; start levodopa?
traps.fix: Withdraw/reduce the offending drug; central anticholinergic (trihexyphenidyl) is used — levodopa is ineffective because D2 receptors are blocked

traps.stem: Thyrotoxic woman in first trimester: drug?
traps.fix: PTU in 1st trimester (carbimazole/methimazole embryopathy: aplasia cutis, choanal atresia), switch to carbimazole in 2nd trimester

cards.text: Vigabatrin is the drug of choice for infantile spasms due to {{c1::tuberous sclerosis}}; its key toxicity is {{c2::irreversible visual field constriction}}

cards.back: Carbamazepine (also phenytoin) – screen in South-East Asian ancestry

cards.front: Class Ic antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in…
cards.back: Structural heart disease / post-MI (↑mortality in CAST trial)

cards.text: Antithyroid drug that also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3: {{c1::propylthiouracil}}; preferred in {{c2::first trimester and thyroid storm}}

cards.front: Diabetes drug class causing euglycaemic DKA and Fournier gangrene
cards.back: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin)

cards.front: Antihypertensive with uricosuric effect, useful in gout
cards.back: Losartan

title: Classic ADRs, unsafe drugs & antidote table
subject: Pharmacology
anchor: Gray baby = chloramphenicol; red man = vancomycin (rate-related histamine release); disulfiram-like = metronidazole, cefoperazone/cefotetan, chlorpropamide, griseofulvin, procarbazine
Gingival hyperplasia = phenytoin, cyclosporine, nifedipine (CCBs)

Glucagon / IV calcium; high-dose insulin euglycaemia

head: Condition
Drugs (classic list)
rows: Primaquine, tafenoquine, dapsone, sulfonamides/cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase, methylene blue, quinolones, naphthalene
Barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, sulfonamides, griseofulvin, rifampicin, oestrogens/OCP, alcohol (treat attack with haemin + glucose)

Warfarin (nasal hypoplasia), ACEi/ARB (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios), isotretinoin, valproate (NTD), thalidomide (phocomelia), lithium (Ebstein), tetracycline (teeth), methotrexate, misoprostol, DES (clear-cell vaginal ca), statins, mycophenolate, streptomycin (8th nerve)

points: **SJS/TEN**: cotrimoxazole/sulfonamides, carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine (↑ with valproate), allopurinol, nevirapine, oxicam NSAIDs
**Ototoxicity**: aminoglycosides (streptomycin vestibular, amikacin/neomycin cochlear), loop diuretics, cisplatin, vancomycin, quinine
**QT prolongation**: class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, ondansetron, haloperidol, TCAs, methadone, azoles, chloroquine/HCQ, bedaquiline
**Gray baby syndrome**: chloramphenicol in neonates – deficient glucuronyl transferase; chloramphenicol also causes idiosyncratic aplastic anaemia
**Red man (vancomycin flushing) reaction**: rapid infusion → non-IgE histamine release; slow infusion over ≥ 1 h + antihistamine
Drug-induced lupus: procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, minocycline, anti-TNF (anti-histone antibodies, spares kidney/CNS)
Rifampicin: orange-red secretions, flu-like syndrome with intermittent dosing, potent enzyme inducer; pyrazinamide: hyperuricaemia
Methylene blue causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency → ascorbic acid / exchange transfusion instead

traps.stem: Flushing and pruritus of upper body during a fast vancomycin infusion
traps.fix: Infusion-rate-related direct mast-cell histamine release (red man); slow the infusion, give antihistamine; not a true allergy

traps.stem: Methaemoglobinaemia in a G6PD-deficient patient – antidote?
traps.fix: Methylene blue needs NADPH (from G6PD) and may cause haemolysis; use ascorbic acid/exchange transfusion/hyperbaric O₂

traps.stem: Which ATT drug is most hepatotoxic?
traps.fix: Pyrazinamide is the most hepatotoxic; rifampicin is the least of the three. Ethambutol is not hepatotoxic (optic neuritis)

cards.front: Antibiotic causing gray baby syndrome and mechanism
cards.back: Chloramphenicol – neonatal deficiency of glucuronyl transferase + poor renal excretion

cards.text: Cephalosporins with N-methylthiotetrazole side chain such as {{c1::cefoperazone / cefotetan}} cause {{c2::disulfiram-like reaction and hypoprothrombinaemia}}

cards.front: Antidote for cyanide poisoning (first-line)
cards.back: Hydroxocobalamin (forms cyanocobalamin); alternative sodium nitrite + sodium thiosulfate

cards.text: Gingival hyperplasia is caused by {{c1::phenytoin}}, {{c2::cyclosporine}} and {{c3::nifedipine/CCBs}}

cards.front: Antidote for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity
cards.back: 20% intravenous lipid emulsion

cards.front: Antitubercular drug causing red-green colour blindness
cards.back: Ethambutol (optic neuritis; caution in young children who cannot report vision)

title: Culture media, stains, biochemical tests & toxigenic bacteria
subject: Microbiology
anchor: TCBS yellow colonies = V. cholerae; tellurite black colonies = C. diphtheriae; Wilson-Blair jet-black metallic sheen = S. Typhi
Albert stain: green bacilli with bluish-black metachromatic granules in Chinese-letter arrangement = C. diphtheriae
Widal: rising (≥ 4-fold) titre in paired sera after week 1; blood culture is the test of choice in week 1

tables.title: Culture media
head: Medium
Type
Organism / feature
rows: Differential (indicator: neutral red) + mildly selective (bile salts)
Lactose fermenters pink (E. coli, Klebsiella mucoid); NLF pale (Salmonella, Shigella, Proteus, Pseudomonas)
V. cholerae yellow (sucrose fermenter); V. parahaemolyticus green
Alkaline peptone water / VR medium / Cary-Blair
M. tuberculosis – rough, buff, 'bread-crumb' colonies in 4–8 weeks
C. diphtheriae – black colonies; Loeffler's serum slope gives growth in 6–8 h
B. pertussis – 'bisected pearl / mercury drop' colonies
S. Typhi – jet-black colonies with metallic sheen

tables.title: Key identification tests
head: Test
Positive organism(s)
Discriminates
rows: Pseudomonas, Vibrio, Neisseria, Campylobacter, H. pylori
Group B Strep (arrowhead haemolysis with S. aureus β-lysin)
GBS vs other β-haemolytic; reverse CAMP = C. perfringens
Proteus, H. pylori, Klebsiella, Cryptococcus, Ureaplasma

points: Gram stain: crystal violet → Gram's iodine (mordant) → decolourise (acetone/alcohol) → safranin counterstain; Gram-positive retain the violet (thick peptidoglycan)

**Ziehl-Neelsen**: hot carbol fuchsin, decolourise with 20% H₂SO₄ (M. tuberculosis) or 5% (M. leprae); 1% H₂SO₄ (modified ZN) for Nocardia, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora; counterstain methylene blue
**Albert stain** (toluidine blue + malachite green): metachromatic (volutin/Babes-Ernst) granules bluish-black, bacilli green; Neisser stain is the alternative

Diphtheria toxin: encoded by β-corynephage (lysogenic conversion); ADP-ribosylates **EF-2**; toxigenicity by **Elek gel precipitation** test; give antitoxin (ADS) on clinical suspicion + penicillin/erythromycin; myocarditis in 2nd week

Tetanus: terminal round spore ('drumstick'); tetanospasmin cleaves synaptobrevin → blocks GABA/glycine release from inhibitory interneurons; trismus earliest sign; HTIG + metronidazole + wound debridement

Cholera: toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs → ↑cAMP; O1 (classical, El Tor) and O139 (Bengal); darting motility inhibited by specific antiserum; rice-water stool; ORS/Ringer lactate + single-dose doxycycline (azithromycin in children/pregnancy)
Enteric fever diagnosis by week (BASU): Blood culture week 1, Antibodies (Widal) week 2, Stool week 3, Urine week 3–4; **bone-marrow culture** most sensitive even after antibiotics

**Widal limitations**: prior vaccination/past infection (H agglutinins persist), anamnestic reaction in other fevers, endemic baseline titres, early antibiotics blunt response, cross-reacting antigens; O antibody rises/falls early, H persists

traps.stem: Day 3 of fever, suspected typhoid; Widal negative
traps.fix: Antibodies appear in week 2; in week 1 do blood culture (bone marrow culture most sensitive). A single Widal has low value; demonstrate 4-fold rise

traps.stem: Medium used for rapid presumptive growth of C. diphtheriae (6–8 h)
traps.fix: Loeffler's serum slope gives rapid growth with good granule formation; tellurite is selective but colonies take ~48 h

traps.stem: Enriched vs enrichment medium
traps.fix: Enriched = solid medium with added nutrients (blood/chocolate agar); enrichment = liquid medium that favours the pathogen over flora (selenite F, alkaline peptone water)

cards.text: V. cholerae forms {{c1::yellow}} colonies on TCBS because it ferments {{c2::sucrose}}

cards.front: Test to detect toxigenicity of C. diphtheriae
cards.back: Elek's gel precipitation (immunodiffusion) test; PCR for tox gene

cards.back: Nocardia, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora (also Rhodococcus, Legionella micdadei)

cards.text: CAMP test is positive with {{c1::Streptococcus agalactiae (GBS)}}; reverse CAMP is positive with {{c2::Clostridium perfringens}}

cards.back: Streptococcus pneumoniae

cards.front: Most sensitive culture for enteric fever (even after antibiotics)
cards.back: Bone-marrow culture

subject: Microbiology
anchor: Weil-Felix: scrub typhus = OX-K only; epidemic/endemic typhus = OX-19 strongly; Q fever, trench fever = negative
C. difficile after antibiotics → GDH + toxin/NAAT → oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin
NTEP: NAAT (CBNAAT/Truenat) upfront for all presumptive TB → detects rifampicin resistance (rpoB)

tables.title: Weil-Felix reaction
head: Disease (agent)
OX-19
OX-2
OX-K
rows: Spotted fevers incl. Indian tick typhus (R. conorii), RMSF

tables.title: Rapid differentiators
head: Organism
Discriminating features
rows: Catalase +, coagulase +, golden colonies, protein A, TSST-1; MRSA = mecA
Bacitracin S, PYR +; ASO high after pharyngitis (low after skin infection → anti-DNase B)
Grows in 6.5% NaCl, bile esculin +, PYR +, intrinsic cephalosporin resistance
Tumbling motility at 25 °C, cold enrichment, neonates/pregnancy/unpasteurised cheese; ampicillin ± gentamicin
Box-car bacilli, 'medusa-head' colonies, McFadyean reaction (capsule), string-of-pearls with penicillin; painless black eschar
Meningococcus ferments glucose + maltose; gonococcus glucose only
Needs X (haemin) + V (NAD); satellitism around S. aureus; Hib capsule = PRP
Oxidase +, non-lactose fermenter, pyocyanin + pyoverdin, grape odour; burns, CF, ecthyma gangrenosum
Mucoid lactose fermenter, non-motile, capsule; currant-jelly sputum
BCYE, urinary antigen (serogroup 1 only), hyponatraemia, diarrhoea, cooling towers
Curved, urease +, oxidase +; urea breath test / stool antigen; MALToma regresses on eradication
Undulant fever, sacroiliitis/spondylitis; Castañeda biphasic medium; doxycycline + rifampicin/aminoglycoside
No cell wall (β-lactams useless), fried-egg colonies, cold agglutinins (IgM anti-I)

points: **C. difficile**: toxin A/B, pseudomembranous colitis after clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones; oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin (metronidazole only if these unavailable); alcohol rub does not kill spores → soap & water

**C. perfringens**: α-toxin (lecithinase, Nagler reaction), double-zone haemolysis, gas gangrene and food poisoning; **botulinum** toxin cleaves SNARE proteins → descending flaccid paralysis with clear sensorium; infant botulism from honey
Bordetella pertussis: pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi → ↑cAMP, marked lymphocytosis; per-nasal swab; azithromycin

**Syphilis**: non-treponemal (VDRL/RPR) for screening & follow-up – biological false positives (SLE, APS, pregnancy, leprosy, malaria), prozone in secondary; treponemal (FTA-ABS, TPHA, TPPA) confirm and stay positive for life; benzathine penicillin; Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
**Leptospirosis**: rat urine, flooding; conjunctival suffusion, calf tenderness; Weil's disease (jaundice + AKI + haemorrhage); MAT is reference serology; EMJH/Korthof media; penicillin/doxycycline
**Scrub typhus**: Orientia tsutsugamushi via larval trombiculid mite (chigger); eschar; IgM ELISA; doxycycline (azithromycin in pregnancy/children)
**Chlamydia**: elementary body (infectious) → reticulate body (replicative); serovars A–C trachoma, D–K genital/inclusion conjunctivitis/neonatal pneumonia, L1–L3 LGV; NAAT; azithromycin/doxycycline
**TB diagnostics (NTEP)**: CBNAAT/Truenat detect MTB + rifampicin resistance; FL-LPA (rpoB, katG, inhA) for INH/RIF; SL-LPA for fluoroquinolone/injectables; liquid culture (MGIT) faster than LJ
**M. leprae**: not cultivable in vitro (mouse foot-pad, nine-banded armadillo); prefers 30–33 °C; slit-skin smear bacteriological index (0–6+); lepromin (Mitsuda) test is prognostic, not diagnostic

traps.stem: Fever with eschar in a farmer; Weil-Felix shows OX-K strongly positive
traps.fix: OX-K alone = scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi); treat with doxycycline

traps.stem: Pyoderma followed by PSGN; ASO titre normal
traps.fix: Skin lipids inactivate streptolysin O, so ASO stays low after impetigo; measure anti-DNase B. Rheumatic fever follows pharyngitis, not skin infection

traps.stem: Lepromin test strongly positive in a patient
traps.fix: Lepromin is a test of CMI and prognosis (positive in TT, negative in LL); it is not diagnostic and is positive in many healthy adults

cards.text: Weil-Felix reaction in scrub typhus is positive only with {{c1::OX-K}}; it is negative in {{c2::Q fever (Coxiella)}}

cards.front: Treponemal test that becomes positive earliest in primary syphilis
cards.back: FTA-ABS (dark-ground microscopy of chancre fluid is the direct test)

cards.front: Organism showing satellitism around S. aureus on blood agar
cards.back: Haemophilus influenzae (needs V factor/NAD released by S. aureus)

cards.text: Listeria shows {{c1::tumbling}} motility at 25 °C and is intrinsically resistant to {{c2::cephalosporins}}

cards.front: Upfront TB test for all presumptive TB in NTEP
cards.back: NAAT – CBNAAT (GeneXpert) or Truenat; also gives rifampicin resistance

Gram-positive cocci in chains – Streptococcus; next step catalase (negative) and haemolysis pattern

verify: Ananthanarayan 12e; IDSA/SHEA 2021 C. difficile update; NTEP Training Modules 2023-24
algorithm:
Gram-positive cocci — identify in this order
→ Catalase test?
  Positive → Staphylococcus: coagulase? Positive → S. aureus (mannitol fermenter); Negative → novobiocin: sensitive = S. epidermidis (biofilm, prosthetic valve), resistant = S. saprophyticus (UTI in young women)
  Negative → Streptococcus: haemolysis on blood agar?
    Beta (clear zone): bacitracin sensitive = Group A (S. pyogenes, PYR+); bacitracin resistant, CAMP +, hippurate + = Group B (S. agalactiae, neonatal sepsis)
    Alpha (green): optochin sensitive, bile soluble = S. pneumoniae; optochin resistant = viridans group (endocarditis)
    Gamma / none: bile esculin positive, grows in 6.5% NaCl = Enterococcus; bile esculin positive, no NaCl growth = Group D non-enterococcus (S. bovis → colon cancer)

title: Virology: hepatitis serology, HIV testing, arboviruses, rabies PEP
subject: Microbiology
anchor: Window period of HBV: HBsAg −, anti-HBs −, only IgM anti-HBc +
HIV diagnosis (NACO): 3 different assays (Strategy III); infant < 18 months → HIV-1 DNA PCR at 6 weeks
Rabies Category III (bite/scratch with bleeding, mucosal/broken-skin lick, bat contact) → wound wash + vaccine + RIG

tables.title: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis
head: Category
Exposure
Action
rows: Touching/feeding animal, licks on intact skin
Nibbling uncovered skin, minor scratches/abrasions without bleeding
Transdermal bites/scratches, licks on broken skin, saliva on mucosa, bat contact
Wound wash + vaccine + RIG (HRIG 20 IU/kg or ERIG 40 IU/kg, infiltrated into wound)
Essen IM: days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28 · Zagreb IM (2-1-1): 2 doses day 0, 1 each day 7 & 21 · Updated Thai Red Cross ID: 2 sites days 0, 3, 7, 28

points: HBV: partially double-stranded DNA with reverse transcriptase; **HBeAg** = infectivity/replication; anti-HBs ≥ 10 mIU/mL protective; newborn of HBsAg+ mother → vaccine + HBIG within 12 h

**HCV**: RNA flavivirus, most become chronic; anti-HCV screen → HCV RNA confirms; pan-genotypic DAA (sofosbuvir + velpatasvir) under NVHCP; extrahepatic: mixed cryoglobulinaemia, MPGN, porphyria cutanea tarda, lichen planus
**HAV/HEV**: faeco-oral, no chronicity in immunocompetent; HEV → fulminant hepatitis with high mortality in 3rd-trimester pregnancy; HDV needs HBsAg (superinfection worse than co-infection)

**HIV**: gp120 binds CD4 + CCR5/CXCR4; gp41 fusion (enfuvirtide); genes gag (p24), pol (RT, integrase, protease), env; 4th-gen ELISA (p24 Ag + Ab) shortens window; viral load monitors ART; first-line NACO = TLD (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir)

Arboviruses: **dengue** (flavivirus, Aedes) NS1 antigen days 1–5, IgM after day 5, secondary infection → severe dengue (antibody-dependent enhancement); **chikungunya** (alphavirus) persistent polyarthralgia; **Zika** microcephaly, GBS; **JE** Culex tritaeniorhynchus, pigs amplifiers, ardeid birds reservoir, live SA-14-14-2 vaccine; **KFD** Haemaphysalis spinigera tick, monkeys amplifiers, Shimoga (Karnataka) 1957, killed vaccine

Herpes: HSV-1 encephalitis (temporal lobe, CSF PCR, IV acyclovir); Tzanck smear multinucleated giant cells; EBV infectious mononucleosis (heterophile/Paul-Bunnell, atypical lymphocytes, CD21 receptor, ampicillin rash); CMV owl's-eye inclusions, commonest congenital infection, periventricular calcification, ganciclovir; HHV-6 roseola; HHV-8 Kaposi sarcoma
Influenza A: segmented negative-sense RNA; **antigenic shift** (reassortment, influenza A only) → pandemics; **drift** (point mutation, A and B) → epidemics; neuraminidase target = oseltamivir

**Rabies**: bullet-shaped rhabdovirus; **Negri bodies** = eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions in Purkinje cells & hippocampal pyramidal cells; ante-mortem: nuchal skin biopsy (hair follicle), corneal impression, saliva RT-PCR; wash wound 15 min with soap and running water, avoid primary suturing
Oncogenic viruses: HPV 16/18 (E6 → p53, E7 → Rb; cervix, oropharynx), EBV (Burkitt, NPC, Hodgkin), HBV/HCV (HCC), HHV-8 (Kaposi, PEL), HTLV-1 (ATLL), Merkel cell polyomavirus

**Nipah**: henipavirus (paramyxovirus), Pteropus fruit bats; date-palm sap/human-to-human spread; encephalitis + respiratory illness, high CFR; Kerala outbreaks since 2018; RT-PCR; **SARS-CoV-2** spike binds ACE2 (TMPRSS2 priming)

traps.fix: Maternal IgG persists up to 18 months; diagnose with HIV-1 DNA PCR (DBS) from 6 weeks

traps.stem: Pandemic influenza arises due to…
traps.fix: Antigenic shift (genetic reassortment of segmented genome, influenza A only); drift causes seasonal epidemics

P. falciparum

points: **Candida albicans**: germ tube within 2 h in serum at 37 °C, chlamydospores on corn-meal agar; **C. auris**: multidrug-resistant, outbreak-prone, misidentified by routine methods → echinocandin
**Cryptococcal meningitis**: CSF CrAg (LFA) most sensitive; induction amphotericin B + flucytosine → fluconazole; manage raised ICP with therapeutic LPs; defer ART 4–6 weeks (IRIS)

**E. histolytica**: trophozoite with ingested RBCs (pathogenic marker), flask-shaped ulcers, quadrinucleate cyst with chromatoid bars; liver abscess (anchovy-sauce pus, right lobe) → metronidazole + luminal agent (paromomycin/diloxanide); E. dispar is a non-pathogenic look-alike
**Giardia**: pear-shaped binucleate trophozoite, ventral sucking disc, 'falling-leaf' motility; duodenum/jejunum → steatorrhoea, malabsorption; IgA deficiency predisposes

**Kala-azar** (L. donovani, Phlebotomus argentipes): LD bodies (amastigotes) in macrophages – splenic aspirate most sensitive; **rK39** rapid test; India: single-dose liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg; PKDL after treatment

**Neurocysticercosis** (eating T. solium EGGS, faeco-oral): stages vesicular (cyst with scolex, 'hole with dot') → colloidal (ring-enhancing, oedema) → granular-nodular → calcified; albendazole ± praziquantel (> 2 cysts) with steroids; antiepileptics; no cysticidal drugs for calcified-only lesions or cysticercal encephalitis; fundoscopy first
**Echinococcus granulosus**: dog definitive, sheep intermediate, man accidental; liver > lung; hydatid sand, daughter cysts, water-lily sign; albendazole + PAIR/surgery; rupture → anaphylaxis

**Autoinfection**: Strongyloides (filariform larvae; hyperinfection with steroids/HTLV-1, Gram-negative sepsis; rhabditiform larvae, not eggs, in stool; ivermectin), Enterobius, Hymenolepis nana, T. solium
**Larva migrans**: cutaneous – Ancylostoma braziliense (creeping eruption); visceral/ocular – Toxocara (eosinophilia; ocular form mimics retinoblastoma); larva currens = Strongyloides

**Filaria**: W. bancrofti (Culex quinquefasciatus, nocturnal periodicity, sheathed, no tail nuclei) vs Brugia malayi (Mansonia, 2 terminal nuclei); ICT antigen card any time of day; tropical pulmonary eosinophilia → DEC 3 weeks; MDA with IDA (ivermectin + DEC + albendazole)

traps.stem: Diabetic in DKA with black nasal eschar; biopsy: broad aseptate right-angled hyphae; started on voriconazole
traps.fix: Mucorales are intrinsically resistant to voriconazole; give liposomal amphotericin B + urgent surgical debridement (posaconazole/isavuconazole step-down)

traps.stem: Person eats undercooked measly pork; risk?
traps.fix: Pork with cysticerci → intestinal taeniasis. Cysticercosis follows ingestion of T. solium EGGS (faeco-oral, including autoinfection from a tapeworm carrier)

traps.trap: P. vivax (most common in many regions)
traps.fix: Banana/crescent gametocytes are diagnostic of P. falciparum; usually only rings and gametocytes circulate (schizonts sequestered)

Key features

First in primary response, largest, most efficient agglutination & complement fixation; cord IgM = intrauterine infection; isohaemagglutinins
Serum monomer; secretory dimer + J chain + secretory component

tables.title: Sterilisation & disinfection
head: Method
Parameters
Use / biological indicator
rows: Surgical instruments, linen, media; Geobacillus stearothermophilus
Glassware, sharp instruments, oils, powders; Bacillus atrophaeus (formerly B. subtilis var niger)
Heat-sensitive plastics, catheters; Bacillus atrophaeus; toxic/carcinogenic
Disposable syringes, gloves, sutures; Bacillus pumilus
Sera, antibiotic & sugar solutions; Brevundimonas diminuta
Milk; Coxiella burnetii is the target; phosphatase test checks adequacy
Sugar & egg media / LJ, Loeffler serum

points: Complement: classical (C1q–IgG/IgM), lectin (MBL–MASP), alternative (spontaneous C3 hydrolysis, factor B, D, properdin) → C3 convertase → C5 convertase → MAC (C5b–9); **C3b** opsonin, **C5a** chemotaxis, C3a/C5a anaphylatoxins
Deficiencies: early classical (C1q, C2, C4) → SLE-like; C3 → recurrent pyogenic infections; C5–C9 → Neisseria; CD55/CD59 → PNH; factor H → aHUS; eculizumab (anti-C5) → give meningococcal vaccine
Live vaccines: BCG, OPV, MR/MMR, rotavirus, varicella, yellow fever (17D), JE SA-14-14-2, Ty21a typhoid, LAIV – avoid in pregnancy/immunosuppression

Killed: IPV, rabies, whole-cell pertussis, KFD, inactivated JE (JENVAC); toxoids: tetanus, diphtheria; subunit/recombinant: hepatitis B (HBsAg), HPV (VLP), acellular pertussis; polysaccharide (T-independent, poor < 2 y): PPSV23, Vi typhoid; conjugate (T-dependent): Hib, PCV, typhoid conjugate
Newer platforms: mRNA (Pfizer/Moderna COVID; India's GEMCOVAC), viral vector (Covishield – ChAdOx1), DNA vaccine ZyCoV-D (India, first human DNA vaccine)

Cold chain: ILR 2–8 °C; most heat-sensitive = OPV; freeze-sensitive = hepatitis B, pentavalent/DPT, Td, PCV, IPV → **shake test** for suspected freezing; VVM inner square matching/darker than outer circle → discard
Open vial policy (India): applies to OPV, DPT, Td, hepatitis B, pentavalent, PCV, IPV (up to 28 days with conditions); reconstituted BCG, MR, JE → discard after 4 h or end of session

Resistance to disinfectants: prions > bacterial spores > mycobacteria > non-enveloped viruses > fungi > vegetative bacteria > enveloped viruses; **Spaulding**: critical → sterilise, semi-critical → HLD, non-critical → low-level

Infection control: WHO 5 moments of hand hygiene (alcohol rub 20–30 s; soap & water for C. difficile spores/norovirus); airborne precautions (TB, measles, varicella – N95, negative-pressure room); droplet (influenza, meningococcus, pertussis, diphtheria); needle-stick seroconversion risk HBV ~30% > HCV ~3% > HIV ~0.3%

BMW Rules 2016 (cross-ref Community Medicine): yellow – anatomical, soiled, cytotoxic, expired drugs, lab cultures → incineration; red – contaminated recyclable plastics (tubing, IV sets, gloves, catheters) → autoclave + shred; white translucent puncture-proof – sharps/needles; blue – glassware & metallic implants

traps.stem: Which immunoglobulin in cord blood indicates congenital infection?
traps.fix: IgM – does not cross the placenta, so its presence means the fetus made it; IgG may be maternal

traps.stem: Recurrent meningococcal meningitis in a young adult; likely defect?
traps.fix: Terminal complement (C5–C9, MAC) deficiency; screen with CH50

algorithm:
Which sterilisation method? Ask: heat stable?
→ Heat-stable
  Moist heat → Autoclave 121 °C, 15 psi, 15 min (sterilises media, linen, surgical instruments; 134 °C 3 min for prions); control: Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores
  Dry heat → Hot-air oven 160 °C for 2 h (glassware, powders, oils); control: Bacillus atrophaeus (subtilis var niger) spores
  Pasteurisation: 72 °C 15 s (HTST) or 63 °C 30 min (holder)
→ Heat-labile
  Ethylene oxide (gas, 30–60 °C) → catheters, endoscopes, plastics; control B. atrophaeus
  Low-temperature hydrogen-peroxide plasma → delicate instruments
  Gamma radiation → disposable plastics, syringes; control Bacillus pumilus
  Filtration (0.22 µm) → heat-labile liquids, serum, antibiotics
→ Chemical high-level disinfection: glutaraldehyde 2% for endoscopes (≥20 min; sterilisation 10 h)
